newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada current account seen swinging into surplus.
newsitem.headline: Canada current account seen swinging into surplus.

text.p: Canada is expected Friday to report its first quarterly surplus on the current account of its balance of payments in 12 years, marking a major turnaround in the country's reliance on foreign capital.
In the long term, analysts said the improvement in Canada's balance of payments will strengthen the currency and make it easier to keep Canadian interest rates low.
"What it really means is we will be less dependent on inflows of foreign capital in the years ahead," said Doug Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns Inc.
The current account is a measure of a country's balance of payments with the rest of the world. It shows that country is paying more to foreigners than it receives from them.

On Friday, Canada is expected to report a current account surplus of C$500 million ($365.9 million U.S.) for the second quarter compared with current account deficit of C$1.94 billion ($1.42 billion) in the first quarter.
It would be the first current account surplus since 1984.

Canada has historically run current account deficits because of its heavy reliance on foreign borrowing. About 40 percent of government debt is held by foreigners, and most of the deficits are the result of interest payments on that debt.

"Interest payments have been flowing out of Canada quite significantly. This is one of the main things that has been pressuring the current account," said Harvinder Kalirai of the New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A.

In 1993, Canada's current account deficit widened to almost C$29 billion ($21.2 billion), or about 4.1 percent of gross domestic product -- the worst performance among the leading industrial nations in the Group of Seven.
Two factors are responsible for the sharp turnaround in the balance of payments, economists said.
First, Canada's merchandise trade surplus has surged in recent years to C$28.4 billion last year. And it is expected to rise even higher this year, according to economists at Bank of Nova Scotia.

At the same time, Canadian governments have sharply reduced their borrowing needs. Seven of Canada's 10 provinces are expected to balance their budgets this year, and the federal government is expected to lower its deficit to C$24.3 billion (US$17.8 billion) in 1996/97.
Increased trade surpluses and lower foreign borrowing means Canada is now likely to begin reporting current account surpluses regularly, economists predicted.
Over the longer term, analysts said this should strengthen the currency and put the Bank of Canada in a better position to keep interest rates low.

"In the past, Canadian interest rates had to be kept relatively high to entice foreign capital inflows," said Kalirai. "With Canada not needing these capital inflows anymore, Canadian interest rates don't have to be kept that high."

A narrowing current account deficit has already made it possible for the Bank of Canada to lower interest rates to well below U.S. levels this year without prompting a selloff in the Canadian dollar, analysts said.
The Bank of Canada has cut interest rates seven times this year. Six of those cuts were made independent of any move by the U.S. Federal Reserve.
